info.desc: Ramones is the debut album by the American punk rock band the Ramones. It was released on April 23, 1976 through Sire Records. Prior to the band signing to Sire, they were seen by Lisa Robinson, an editor of Hit Parader, during an early 1975 performance. Robinson began popularizing the band by writing about them in the magazines she edited. Robinson contacted Danny Fields and asked him to manage the band, which he agreed to in November 1975. A Marty Thau produced demo album was recorded at 914 Sound Studios and included "Judy Is a Punk" and "I Wanna Be .

podcast.body: Recorded at a studio in Radio City Music Hall, the album sessions began on February 2, 1976, and were completed by February 19, 1976, costing a total of $6,400. Legend states the master tape was so loud it irreparably damaged the pressing equipment, "blowing the cutter head clean off the machine." Upon its release on April 23, 1976, it was largely treated as a joke due to its fourteen two-minute songs, 28-minute length, and lack of guitar solos. However, it was also understood by some as embodying "the unpretentious joy of making rock and roll" with raw "energy, enthusiasm, the passion, and the realness of it all." "When the album was released on April 23rd, 1976, almost everyone treated this record as some kind of joke."

podcast.body: This self-titled debut album clocked in at just under 30 minutes and was released in England before its US debut. It featured one of their few covers, Chris Montez's 1962 song "Let's Dance," which exemplified their approach of reclaiming and stripping down rock music, then speeding it up and making it their own, hinting at the sound of 1980s new wave. "Their self-titled debut clocked in at just under 30 minutes One of their very few covers showed how the Ramones were kind of reclaiming Rather than rejecting rock music, stripping it down and then speeding it up and making it their own."

podcast.title: Debut Album
podcast.body: Recorded from February 2nd to February 19th, 1976, at Plaza City Sound, a large studio on the 8th floor of Radio City Music Hall. The total cost for recording was $6,400, which was $400 more than their advance. When the master was sent to the record plant, it was so loud that it blew a cutter head right off the machine. The album was released on April 23rd, 1976. Its cover photo, featuring the band against a brick wall, is now considered an all-time rock and roll classic, taken by photographer Roberta Bailey near CBGB. Critical reception was mixed, and almost no radio station would play it, but it became highly influential in the UK. The album finally sold over 500,000 copies in early 2014, earning a gold record status. "The cover photo of the band's Denny against a brick wall was now considered to be an all-time rock and roll classic."

podcast.title: Self-Titled Debut
podcast.body: Released on April 23, 1976, this album features a simple black and white photograph of the four band members in ripped jeans and leather jackets, posed against a graffiti-covered brick wall. This aesthetic was intended to represent the band as a unified "gang." The photo was taken by Roberta Bailey for *Punk Magazine* and was chosen after the band's initial preference for a style resembling The Beatles' *Meet the Beatles* (1964) was rejected by Sire Records art director Tony Wadler. The image was taken in Albert's Garden, a private community garden in New York City, and manager Danny Fields approved of its perfection. The cover helped solidify a distinctive punk-fashion look and has since become one of the most imitated album poses, even becoming part of the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York. "This is a perfect representation of the band as a gang aesthetic."
